task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of August 6, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style newspaper update on Moorlace Broadband Cooperative's construction award and the premises left outside its first fiber build.

facts.text: Moorlace Broadband Cooperative awarded its first fiber construction contract on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, to Pella Trenchworks.
The $8.4 million phase is financed by a $5 million rural-infrastructure grant and a $3.4 million cooperative loan.
The contracted route passes 620 premises: 240 businesses and 380 homes.
An earlier proposed route covered 790 premises, including 170 farms and homes beyond the Greyfin road bridge.
The bridge owner has not approved attaching a cable conduit, leaving the 170 premises outside the signed contract.
The cooperative has requested an engineering study of an alternative river crossing but has no construction price for it.
Construction is scheduled to begin Sept. 14, with the first connections expected in spring 2027.
A property passed by the cable is not automatically connected; its owner must order service and approve installation.
The cooperative's announced residential package costs $59 a month, with a $149 standard installation charge.
A business package with priority fault response is separately priced at $95 a month.
General manager Daro Senn said actual service dates will depend on road-opening permits and property access.
Senn said, "Signing the trenching contract gives us a route to build, not a date for every front door."
Farm-equipment dealer Neri Voss currently carries large diagnostic files to a supplier on a portable drive because uploads are unreliable.
Voss's workshop is on the contracted side of the river, while several customers who need remote diagnostics are beyond the bridge.
Farmer Yara Tern said, "I helped sign people up for this, and I am still on the far side of the map."
Members beyond the bridge retain voting rights and will not be billed for broadband service before a connection is installed.
The cooperative has 412 members, a membership count that does not equal the number of premises in either route.
Existing wireless providers will continue operating; the new contract does not require residents to switch.
The cooperative formed in 2022 after a group of small employers surveyed problems sending payroll and design files.
No performance tests on the unbuilt fiber network or estimates of household savings have been released.
